# Loss Functions {#sec-Loss_Functions}
A loss function $L(y, \hat y)$ quantifies the discrepancy between an observed value $y$ and a prediction $\hat{y} = f(x)$. It turns the abstract goal of "fitting the data well" into a concrete objective that a learning algorithm can minimize. Training a model amounts to choosing $f$ from some class of functions so as to make the accumulated loss small.

Because the true data generating distribution is typically unknown, models minimize the empirical risk, i.e. the average loss over the observed data:
$$
\hat{R}(f) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i = 1}^{n} L\left(y_i, f(x_i)\right),
$$
which approximates the (unknown) expected risk $\E{L(y, \hat{y})}$. The choice of loss encodes what kind of errors matter: it determines the optimal prediction, how sensitive the fit is to outliers, and how the resulting optimization behaves. The appropriate loss depends primarily on whether the task is regression (continuous $y$) or classification (categorical $y$).
